source.title_on_document: Generative AI-Supported Creative Writing Among Primary School Students: A Study of Creative Writing Performance, Writing Self-Efficacy, and Flow State

supplement.where: The document cites no supplementary material or online appendix.
supplement.holds: Nothing known. All reported statistics (Tables 1 to 4) are in the main text.

paper_design_summary: 78 fifth-grade students from three classes at one primary school in eastern China were assigned to write a roughly 300-word essay (Design Future Cars) in 25 minutes with Deepseek (n = 20), with a peer (n = 38, 19 pairs), or alone (n = 20); a week earlier all wrote a baseline essay alone. Three researchers scored the handwritten essays on a 100-point rubric (originality 40, flexibility 30, elaboration 30), and students completed self-report flow and writing self-efficacy scales.

studies.label: Classroom experiment (essay writing with GenAI, with a peer, or alone)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Writing condition: GenAI-supported writing (Deepseek), peer-collaborative writing (pairs), or individual writing
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three experimental conditions: (1) GenAI-supported writing group (n=20), in which students used GenAI to support the creative-writing task

arms.name: GenAI-supported writing group
arms.description: Each student wrote with Deepseek on a computer (after a tutorial to use it as a thinking partner and not copy verbatim), then wrote the final essay by hand

arms.name: Peer-collaborative writing group
arms.description: Students paired to write the essay collaboratively (19 pairs), by hand

arms.name: Individual writing group
arms.description: Each student wrote the essay alone, by hand

participants.exclusions: None stated. The paper says no students or parents declined after consent; Table 1 reports N = 20, 38, 20, summing to the 78 assigned.
participants.who: Fifth-grade primary school students aged 10-12 (M = 11, SD = 0.51), 42 boys and 36 girls, from three classes taught by the same teacher, recruited by convenience sampling; already familiar with GenAI tools
participants.quote: A total of 78 students (aged 10–12 years; M=11, SD=0.51) from three classes were invited to participate in the study.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 3.1; p. 5, Figure 1; p. 7, Table 1

ai_tool.how_used: Students prompted Deepseek on a computer during the 25-minute writing task, instructed to use it as a thinking partner and to consider, select, and revise its suggestions; final essays were handwritten. Logs show 50 task-related prompts from 20 students (mean 2.50 per student), mostly idea generation (54%) and idea elaboration (20%) (p. 6 Section 3.4; p. 8 Section 4.4, Table 4).

task.description: Essay of about 300 words, 'Design Future Cars' (week 2 experimental task); week 1 baseline task 'Design Future Shoes' written alone by all. Authors note the task leaned toward expository and informational writing (p. 10).
task.duration: 25 min per essay; experiment spanned 2 weeks

outcomes.name: Creative writing performance (total rubric score, 0-100)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Three researchers scored each essay on a rubric: originality (40 points), flexibility (30), elaboration (30), total 100. Week-2 Kendall's W = 0.89 and the average of raters was used; week-1 W = 0.57, resolved by consensus discussion (p. 6, Section 3.4). Dimension subscores are not reported separately. Raters are researchers; blinding to condition not stated.

contrasts.reported: GenAI-supported writing group (a) N = 20, Mean 88.850, SD 1.420; Individual writing group (c) N = 20, Mean 85.133, SD 2.120. Omnibus one-way ANOVA across three groups F = 13.095, p = 0.000***, Partial η2 = 0.259, Cohen's f = 0.591; LSD a > c (pairwise p not printed)

GenAI-supported writing group (a) N = 20, Mean 88.850, SD 1.420; Peer-collaborative group (b) N = 38, Mean 86.825, SD 2.719. Omnibus F = 13.095, p = 0.000***, Partial η2 = 0.259, Cohen's f = 0.591; LSD a > b (pairwise p not printed)

eligibility.reason: The paper states individual random assignment of 78 students to GenAI, peer, or individual writing (p. 4), and researchers scored the essays written with AI available on a creativity rubric (p. 6, p. 7 Table 1). The study has 78 people across arms, but the GenAI vs individual contrast has only 40 and GenAI vs peer 58; students came from three intact classes, and the paper does not say how class membership relates to the arms.

one_line_finding: Fifth graders writing with Deepseek scored 88.850 (SD 1.420, n = 20) on a 100-point creativity rubric, versus 86.825 (SD 2.719, n = 38) with a peer and 85.133 (SD 2.120, n = 20) alone; omnibus F = 13.095, p < 0.001, LSD GenAI > both (p. 7, Table 1).
open_questions: Students came from three classes; the paper says assignment was random but does not say whether it was at the student level within classes or whether classes mapped to conditions.
In the peer arm, 19 pairs wrote collaboratively, yet Table 1 lists N = 38; the paper does not say whether each pair's essay score was counted once per student.
Pairwise post hoc (LSD) p-values and standard errors are not printed; only the omnibus F, p, partial eta squared, and Cohen's f.
Raters were the researchers; the paper does not say whether they were blind to condition.
Baseline (week 1, written alone) scores are reported only as an omnibus ANOVA (F = 2.56, p > 0.05); arm means are not given.
notes: Self-reported outcomes not listed as outcomes because they are not scored on output: Writing Self-Efficacy Scale (GenAI 5.276, SD 0.342; peer 5.022, SD 0.756; individual 4.812, SD 0.708; Welch F = 4.106, p = 0.023; LSD a > c; p. 7 Table 2) and Flow Status Scale (GenAI 3.919, SD 0.441; peer 4.428, SD 0.540; individual 4.031, SD 0.635; F = 6.974, p = 0.002; LSD b > c, b > a; p. 8 Table 3). The descriptive interaction-log analysis (Table 4, 50 episodes) is not a creativity outcome. Design coded field_rct because the sessions took place during regular class hours in the school's computer lab with three researchers monitoring; lab_rct is a defensible alternative. The authors stress that GenAI-group scores reflect AI-supported products, not unaided writing ability (p. 8).
